name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: Pupils clean the school
items.fact: In most Japanese schools, there are no cleaners for the classrooms: after lessons, pupils sweep the floors, wipe the desks and clean the corridors and even the toilets themselves.

items.name: No planes during the exam
items.fact: On the day of South Korea’s university entrance exam, planes are stopped from taking off and landing during the English listening test, so that the noise doesn’t disturb the candidates.

items.name: Chess on the timetable
items.fact: In 2011, Armenia became the first country to make chess a compulsory school subject. Primary pupils have chess lessons as part of their normal timetable.

items.name: Eye exercises
items.fact: Pupils in China do eye exercises in class every day, massaging the points around their eyes to recorded music and instructions, to protect their eyesight.

items.name: The school nap
items.fact: Many Chinese primary schools have a midday nap: after lunch, pupils rest for a while, often with their heads on their desks or, in some schools, on desks and chairs that fold out into small beds.

items.name: A break every 45 minutes
items.fact: In Finland, primary pupils usually get a 15-minute break after every 45 minutes of lessons, and they go outside to play in almost any weather, even in the snow.

items.name: A cycling exam
items.fact: Dutch children take a traffic exam at primary school, around the age of 10 or 11, which often includes a practical test on their bikes on real roads.

items.name: The pen licence
items.fact: In many German primary schools, children have to earn a “pen licence” before they are allowed to write with a fountain pen instead of a pencil.

items.name: Whistling lessons
items.fact: On La Gomera, in the Canary Islands, schoolchildren have to learn Silbo, a whistled language that shepherds used to send messages across the island’s deep valleys.

items.name: The tattie holidays
items.fact: In Scotland, many people still call the October school holiday the “tattie holidays”, because children were once given time off school to help farmers pick the potato harvest.

fakes.name: The shoelace test
fakes.fact: Belgian children must pass a short shoelace test before they start primary school. Those who fail get a practice shoe to take home over the summer.

fakes.name: Reading hats
fakes.fact: Polish primary pupils wear coloured caps that show their reading level, from yellow to dark blue, so that older pupils know who to help in the library.

fakes.name: Exam-day bananas
fakes.fact: A Hungarian law says that schools must give every pupil a free banana on the morning of a national exam, after a study suggested that it helped concentration.

fakes.name: Grandparent lessons
fakes.fact: Portuguese primary schools must invite a grandparent to teach one lesson each term, on anything from fishing to old songs. Schools get a small grant to pay for the coffee.

fakes.name: The homework lottery
fakes.fact: In many Danish primary schools, homework is set by lottery: every Monday, one pupil draws a card from a box, and the card decides which subject gets homework that week.

fakes.name: The singing exam
fakes.fact: To leave secondary school in Lithuania, every pupil must pass a short singing exam: one folk song, sung alone in front of two teachers. Nobody has ever failed.

fakes.name: A pen-pal by law
fakes.fact: Irish primary pupils must write a handwritten letter every term to a pen-pal in a school in another county. The post office delivers the letters for free.

fakes.name: The birthday desk
fakes.fact: In Latvian primary schools, a pupil on their birthday sits at the teacher’s desk for the whole day, and the teacher sits in the pupil’s place.

fakes.name: Name-day holiday
fakes.fact: Greek pupils get the day off school on their name day, the feast day of the saint they are named after. Children called Maria or Giorgos get the most days off.

fakes.name: Ringing the bell
fakes.fact: In Romanian schools, the pupil with the best marks of the week rings the school bell by hand at the start and end of every break the following week.
